video_title: The AI Price War Nobody Saw Coming with FirstMark's David Waltcher
gist: FirstMark partner David Waltcher tells Dan Nathan that 2026 is the year enterprises stop 'token maxing' — routing every task to the most expensive frontier model — as Chinese and open-weight models (GLM, MiniMax, Kimi, Qwen) priced at roughly 1/20th per million tokens flipped OpenRouter's closed/open token mix in February 2026 and forced frontier pricing down. He is 'largely bearish on the application layer' yet argues incumbents like Salesforce are more durable than public markets assume, sees an unusually rich M&A window (Stripe/OpenRouter at $7B, Silver Lake circling Workday, Google/Wiz at $32B), and has put his last three investments entirely into AI security (Onyx Security, Nebulock, Tracebit).

themes.theme: Token maxing and the model price war

insights.claim: FirstMark's David Waltcher predicts 2026 will be the year companies confront whether 'token maxing' — defaulting every task to the largest, most expensive frontier model — is economically defensible, and expects the free market to force routing discipline.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: If enterprise token spend shifts from 'always frontier' to task-tiered routing, revenue-per-seat assumptions embedded in frontier-lab valuations and in AI-native app pricing need to be re-underwritten.
insights.quote: I think 2026 will among many things be a year where companies sort of face the truth about whether token maxing is something they want to be doing or not or at least in what capacity.

insights.claim: Waltcher argues the token-maxing pricing mismatch is exposed by a simple labor analogy: code-gen companies paying 50th-to-60th percentile salaries for engineers are simultaneously paying 100th percentile prices for tokens.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: A clean heuristic for spotting AI-native startups with structurally unsustainable COGS — gross margins compress unless they downshift models, so watch for routing adoption as a margin catalyst.
insights.quote: Why are they paying 100 percentile for tokens? Why are they using the most expensive biggest and best models for a variety of tasks, some of which actually don't require that level of intelligence?

insights.claim: Waltcher claims the vast majority of a developer's daily tasks — opening a PR, doing code review — do not require the latest Opus-class model, making frontier intelligence overkill for routine enterprise work.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: The addressable volume for cheap mid-tier and open models is far larger than the frontier-benchmark narrative implies; inference providers and gateway layers capture that spread.
insights.quote: Many of those individual tasks do not require the latest Opus model, right?

insights.claim: Waltcher contends the industry's benchmark obsession is misaligned with enterprise buying, because benchmarks measure impressive model characteristics that are largely irrelevant to what people do in their day jobs.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: Benchmark leadership announcements are a weak predictor of enterprise revenue share; price-per-useful-task is the metric to track instead.
insights.quote: we're in this benchmark world and many of these benchmarks are increasingly like very of impressive things that suggest a whole slew of of characteristics about a model, many of which are really, really important, but for people to do their day job are not highly relevant.

insights.claim: Waltcher notes that in roughly February 2026, OpenRouter's token mix flipped from about 60/40 closed-versus-open to open-model majority as GLM, MiniMax, Kimi and Qwen gained share.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: OpenRouter's public token-share data is a real-time leading indicator of frontier-lab pricing power erosion — a free dataset for tracking the commoditization thesis.
insights.quote: I think it was roughly 60/40 closed open, and it completely flipped. And the open models had this moment.

insights.claim: Waltcher says the open models that took share were priced at roughly one-twentieth the cost per million tokens of closed frontier models while remaining highly performant on everyday tasks.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: A 20x price gap at comparable everyday performance is the mechanism behind the price war; it caps how much frontier labs can charge for undifferentiated workloads.
insights.quote: these models were basically 1/20th of the token cost per million tokens, and they were highly performant at a lot of the things that people do in their every day

insights.claim: Model gateways and routers that dynamically load-balance tasks across models in real time are the enabling infrastructure of the price war, according to Waltcher, and are why OpenRouter became strategically valuable.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: The routing/gateway layer is a toll booth on model commoditization — a category worth screening for both private investment and acquisition premiums.

insights.claim: Dan Nathan argues Chinese open-source models are directly causing a price war, citing a roughly 70% price cut on the newest flagship model as evidence, and warns this creates a problem for labs preparing to IPO.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan (host)
insights.so_what: If frontier pricing is being set by Chinese open-weight competition rather than by capability, pre-IPO revenue quality at the labs is lower than headline growth suggests.
insights.quote: So, the Chinese open-source models are causing a price war here.

insights.claim: Waltcher believes demand for maximum frontier intelligence is effectively unbounded and will persist even as routine workloads commoditize, because each new best-in-class model release absorbs whatever supply exists.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: Argues for a barbell outcome — frontier compute demand stays tight while the mid-tier commoditizes — supporting continued capex even amid price deflation.
insights.quote: I don't know if the like demand being infinite for max intelligence will ever go away.

themes.theme: China's capex asymmetry and the closing model gap

insights.claim: Dan Nathan contrasts Alibaba's three-year capex guidance of $56 billion against roughly $800 billion of hyperscaler capex this year and about $1.5 trillion next year, framing China's AI buildout as radically more capital-efficient.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan (host)
insights.so_what: If Chinese labs close the capability gap on ~1-2% of US capex, the US hyperscaler capex cycle carries real misallocation risk that current semis and power valuations do not price.
insights.quote: Alibaba guided for the next 3 years for CapEx, 56 billion dollars. Our companies, the four hyperscalers, are going to spend 800 billion dollars this year.

insights.claim: Nathan argues Chinese labs are innovating around export controls by using less power-intensive chips and domestic memory such as CXMT, since they cannot access Blackwell-class GPUs or high-bandwidth memory.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan (host)
insights.so_what: Export controls are pushing China toward a domestic memory and compute stack — a structural share risk for US HBM/DRAM suppliers over time even as it slows Chinese training near-term.

insights.claim: Nathan identifies cheaper cost of capital, labor and energy plus state backing — with Chinese energy capacity growing much faster than in the US — as the inputs letting China compress the model gap.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan (host)
insights.so_what: Energy availability, not chips alone, becomes the binding constraint to watch in the US AI buildout; power infrastructure is the bottleneck trade.

insights.claim: Despite the Chinese cost advantage, Waltcher maintains that the most valuable companies in the broader AI universe are American and will remain so for quite some time.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: A direct pushback on the 'China wins AI' trade — value accrual and capability leadership can decouple, so cheap Chinese models can pressure pricing without displacing US equity value.
insights.quote: The most valuable companies in the broader AI universe are American-based, and that will be true for I think quite some time.

insights.claim: Nathan frames Microsoft Copilot as the natural distribution channel for cheap models, noting roughly 450 million Office 365 users of which only about 20 million have converted to Copilot.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan (host)
insights.so_what: A ~4% Copilot attach rate means Microsoft's incentive is to bundle cheaper third-party models to drive conversion — bearish for OpenAI's pricing leverage inside Microsoft's stack.

themes.theme: Application-layer durability vs. the SaaS-is-dead trade

insights.claim: Waltcher holds a two-sided view: he is largely bearish on the application layer overall but believes individual incumbents will prove more durable than public-market investors assume, producing a haves/have-nots split driven by adaptability, entrenchment and switching costs.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: Suggests pair-trading within SaaS rather than shorting the index — differentiate on system-of-record status and switching costs instead of applying a blanket AI-disruption discount.
insights.quote: I am I am largely bearish on the application layer. I also think that a lot of these companies are going to be more durable than many in the public market think

insights.claim: Waltcher argues a vibe-coded CRM clone is irrelevant to displacing Salesforce because the moat is the partner ecosystem, custom implementations, and decade-long trust relationships rather than the front-end application.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete test for which SaaS names survive AI: score the ecosystem and implementation depth, not UI replicability, before pricing in disruption.
insights.quote: whether or not I could vibe code a CRM has actually very little to do with whether I could duplicate that business, right?

insights.claim: Waltcher expects human interaction with systems of record to fall sharply while agentic interaction rises, leaving open whether vendors like Salesforce can still command the same contract-size premium.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: Seat-based pricing is the exposed variable, not customer retention — watch net revenue retention and per-contract value at CRM/HRIS/ITSM vendors for the first evidence.

insights.claim: Waltcher reports that very large AI companies are themselves signing contracts today with legacy category leaders in CRM, HRIS and IT help desk, evidence that scaled operations still require these systems of record.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: AI-native companies buying legacy SaaS is a direct counter-datapoint to the churn thesis and a bullish tell for incumbent bookings.

insights.claim: Waltcher observes the public market repeatedly makes very strong moves on very little information in AI, citing an episode roughly five months earlier where a viral vibe-coding post about a customer-support tool whacked the SaaS index that day.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: Engagement-optimized social narratives create recurring, mean-reverting dislocations in SaaS — a tradable pattern for those who can distinguish narrative from fundamentals.
insights.quote: you see very strong reactions with very little information in the public markets often

insights.claim: Waltcher and Nathan flag Stripe's acquisition of OpenRouter — which raised in May at a $1.3 billion valuation and sold for $7 billion — as the marquee example of AI-era M&A premiums.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan (host)
insights.so_what: A ~5x markup within months sets the comp for model-routing and AI-infrastructure assets and signals how aggressively well-capitalized private buyers will pay for strategic positioning.
insights.quote: raised in May at $1.3 billion and it just got bought for $7 billion

insights.claim: Waltcher attributes the current M&A wave to three converging forces: public-market volatility creating cheap assets like Workday, previous-era winners such as Stripe buying from a position of strength, and a new class of extremely well-capitalized AI buyers.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: A three-factor screen for identifying the next targets: depressed public multiples plus a strategic gap plus a buyer with balance-sheet firepower.

insights.claim: Nathan notes Silver Lake and another party kicking the tires on Workday, a roughly $40-45 billion market-cap company where even a 20% premium would still leave the price about 40% below its all-time high.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan (host)
insights.so_what: Beaten-down large-cap SaaS is now within reach of financial buyers — a screenable setup for takeout optionality across the de-rated enterprise software complex.

insights.claim: Waltcher cites a $60 billion figure for Cursor as evidence that AI-era acquirers are already large enough to absorb outcomes that would have been unthinkable in prior cycles, alongside increasingly aggressive hyperscalers and Datadog.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: Exit ceilings for AI startups have moved up an order of magnitude, which changes venture return math and justifies higher entry valuations at seed and Series A.

insights.claim: Waltcher points to Salesforce's acquisition of Momentum — his first FirstMark investment, which synthesizes live meeting notes into Salesforce — as the template for incumbents buying their way out of the data-entry problem.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific acquisition thesis for systems of record: buy the agentic capture layer, because reps using 20 AI tools will no longer spend two hours a day on manual input.

insights.claim: Waltcher says security has been one of the most active M&A markets for as long as it has existed and that private security transactions tend to close at richer multiples than infrastructure or software counterparts, predicting substantial further consolidation.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: Security startups carry a structural multiple premium on exit — relevant both to venture allocation and to anticipating buyer behavior after Google's $32 billion Wiz deal.
insights.quote: There's a reason security's been one of the most active M&A markets for as long as it's existed, right?

themes.theme: AI security: agents as the new attack surface

insights.claim: Waltcher says security's paradigm has shifted because vulnerability counts have ballooned and effectively everything is becoming a zero day, collapsing the window between disclosure and exploitation to a point human security teams cannot defend.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: Compressed exploit windows force automation spend regardless of IT budget cycles, making AI-security a non-discretionary line item and a defensive growth vector.
insights.quote: the number of vulnerabilities has ballooned. And also just everything's becoming a zero day.

insights.claim: Waltcher argues security is ceasing to function as an insurance-like industry because attack activity across endpoints, cloud services and firewalls has escalated beyond historical norms, with incidents like the Hugging Face/OpenAI agent breach recurring weekly.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: Reframes security spend from a cost-of-doing-business insurance premium to an operational necessity, supporting multiple expansion for vendors that credibly ship AI defenses.

insights.claim: Waltcher has concentrated his last three investments entirely in security — Onyx Security for agent inventory and semantic runtime guardrails, Nebulock for agentic threat hunting, and Tracebit for deception canaries under an 'assumed breach' mindset.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: Maps the three emerging AI-security subcategories a public investor should expect incumbents to acquire: agent governance, autonomous threat hunting, and post-breach deception.
insights.quote: my last three investments have all been security investments.

insights.claim: Waltcher frames AI agents as a distinct vulnerability class because they operate stochastically, act far faster than humans, and hold credentials and system access that even the people who provisioned them do not fully understand.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: Agent inventory and runtime guardrails become a mandatory new budget line for CISOs — a greenfield category with no incumbent owner yet.

insights.claim: Waltcher cites that roughly 95% of breaches are now credentialed, which he says exposes the failure of the zero-trust paradigm and justifies Tracebit's assumed-breach, honeypot-based approach.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: Undermines the investment case for identity-and-authentication-centric security and shifts value toward detection, deception and response speed.
insights.quote: Something like 95% of breaches now are credentialed.

insights.claim: Waltcher expects CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks to win the AI-security era rather than be disrupted by it, because the breadth of customer resources they already touch converts into an immediate buyer queue for any compelling AI security product.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: Distribution and trust, not product novelty, determine the winners — supports owning the platform incumbents alongside, not against, the AI-security startup wave.
insights.quote: these are winners of the SaaS era who are now winners of the AI era

themes.theme: Market structure, AGI skepticism and downside risks

insights.claim: Waltcher rejects the winner-take-all framing for AI and calls the 'Anthropic wins enterprise, OpenAI wins consumer' split lazy, pointing to OpenAI's Codex numbers as evidence both are performing strongly across segments.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: Argues against concentrating exposure in a single lab on segment-narrative grounds; leadership rotates with each model and product release.
insights.quote: I even think like comments about Anthropic being the enterprise winner and OpenAI being the consumer winner are a bit lazy.

insights.claim: Waltcher believes the enterprise market is too vast and too vertical-specific for any single lab to take, citing FirstMark portfolio companies Legora in legal and Nebulock in threat hunting that build proprietary agent harnesses on top of frontier models.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: Supports the vertical-AI application thesis at seed and Series A despite lab platform risk — the analogy is open-source and cloud dependency, which never prevented durable company building.

insights.claim: Waltcher's stated primary derailment risk is macro rather than technological: a major public-market crash or recession would cut LP allocations as public portfolios shrink roughly 30%, making venture look comparatively overweight and stalling new fund commitments with a lag.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: The denominator effect, not AI capability plateaus, is the transmission channel from a public drawdown to a private AI funding freeze — watch LP allocations as the early warning.

insights.claim: Waltcher takes a realist stance on AGI, arguing that even if innovation froze today there would be enormous value left to create because adoption is very early across industries and geographies.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: Decouples the AI investment case from AGI timelines — a hedge against disappointment if lab leaders keep pushing out grandiose milestone claims.
insights.quote: I think if the world froze today from an innovation standpoint there would be so much value still to be created in AI.

insights.claim: Waltcher says continued improvement across cost, speed, performance and capability is sufficient on its own to sustain a massive supercycle in company creation, independent of whether AGI is reached.
insights.speaker: David Waltcher
insights.so_what: Gives four concrete trajectory variables to monitor as the actual invalidation test for the AI cycle, rather than binary AGI declarations.
insights.quote: as long as we are on the trajectory that we are on which looks like model improvement across cost, speed, performance, capability you are just going to see a massive super cycle like the one that we're in

insights.claim: Nathan pitches Zoom as an underappreciated takeout candidate, citing a large installed base, high switching costs, weak competitive alternatives in Google Meet and Microsoft Teams, no debt, and a valuation around 2x cash.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan (host)
insights.so_what: A specific de-rated SaaS name Nathan flags as an M&A target, though he explicitly notes he does not own it.
insights.quote: I think they're trading at like 2x cash or something like that. There's no debt
